subject: ai
question: Can the team expect performance close to mAP 0.89 at night?

artifact.explanation:
A pedestrian detector was trained and tested on 50,000 daytime street images (test mAP 0.89).
Plan: deploy it on night-time CCTV footage.

ai_claim: Yes. The model reached 0.89 on held-out images, so it detects pedestrians reliably and will work at night too.

ai_solution.text: Test mAP is 0.89.
Test images were held out.
Pedestrians look the same day or night.
So night-time performance will be similar.

failure.misconception: Assuming the visual conditions do not matter
failure.explanation: Night footage has low light, noise, glare from headlights and often infrared greyscale - all absent from training. Pedestrians do not look the same to a model trained only on daylight. Evaluate on labelled night footage and add night data (or domain adaptation) before deployment.
failure.why_convincing: The objects are the same; the conditions are what changed.

canonical_solution: No: night footage is a different visual domain. Evaluate on night data and train with it.

valid_evidence.summary: All 50,000 training and test images are daytime.
In infrared CCTV, pedestrians appear as bright greyscale shapes unlike any training image.

hints.text: Compare the training conditions with deployment conditions.
Step 3 assumes appearance is unchanged.
Visual domain shift (lighting, sensor) degrades vision models.
Test on night footage.
Step 3 is wrong: night images differ greatly. Evaluate and train on them.

repair: Collect and label night footage for evaluation and training.
debrief: Vision models learn pixels, not concepts. Lighting, sensors and weather are part of the input distribution.

subject: ai
question: Does the prediction count as a correct detection under this benchmark?

artifact.explanation:
Ground-truth box: x 0-10, y 0-10.
Predicted box: x 5-15, y 0-10.
The benchmark counts a detection as correct at IoU >= 0.5.
AI: "The boxes overlap substantially, so this is a correct detection."

ai_claim: Yes. Half of the ground-truth box is covered by the prediction, so the overlap meets the 0.5 threshold.

ai_solution.text: The boxes overlap in x from 5 to 10.
Half of the ground-truth box is covered.
That is an overlap of 0.5.
So it counts as correct.

failure.misconception: Confusing coverage with intersection over union
failure.explanation: IoU divides the intersection by the union, not by the ground-truth area. Intersection = 5 x 10 = 50; union = 100 + 100 - 50 = 150; IoU = 0.33, below 0.5. The detection counts as a false positive (and the object as missed).
failure.why_convincing: Half the ground truth really is covered.

canonical_solution: IoU = 50 / 150 = 0.33 < 0.5, so it is not a correct detection.

valid_evidence.summary: IoU = area(A intersect B) / area(A union B).

hints.text: Compute the union of the two boxes.
Step 3 divides by the wrong area.
IoU uses the union as the denominator.
Step 3 is wrong: IoU is 0.33, below 0.5.

debrief: Detection metrics depend on precise overlap definitions. Coverage of the ground truth ignores how much the prediction spills outside it.

subject: ai
question: Does AUC 0.95 show the model recognises pneumonia?

artifact.explanation:
A pneumonia classifier trained on X-rays from two hospitals reaches AUC 0.95.
Saliency maps show the model focuses on a metal token in the image corner that differs between hospitals. Hospital B treats far more pneumonia cases.
AI: "AUC 0.95 shows the model has learned to recognise pneumonia."

ai_claim: Yes. The model separates pneumonia from normal X-rays with AUC 0.95, so it has learned to recognise pneumonia.

ai_solution.text: AUC is 0.95 on the test set.
The test set contains pneumonia and normal X-rays.
High AUC means the model separates the classes using disease features.
So it recognises pneumonia.

failure.misconception: Assuming high accuracy means the intended features were learned
failure.explanation: The model can separate classes by recognising which hospital an image came from (the corner token), because hospital B has more pneumonia cases. That shortcut works on test data from the same hospitals and fails elsewhere. Test on images from a new hospital, mask the token, and inspect what the model uses.
failure.why_convincing: The AUC is real and high.

canonical_solution: No: the model may be detecting the hospital, not the disease. Validate on an external hospital with the token masked.

valid_evidence.summary: Saliency focuses on the corner token that identifies the hospital.
On a third hospital's X-rays, AUC drops to 0.68.

counterexamples: Masking the corner token lowers performance sharply.

hints.text: Look at what the model attends to.
Step 3 assumes disease features were used.
Models exploit any feature correlated with the label, including artefacts.
Evaluate on a new hospital.
Step 3 is wrong: the model may use the hospital token as a shortcut.

repair: Mask artefacts, balance cases across hospitals, and validate externally.
debrief: Shortcut learning is common in vision. External validation is the most reliable way to detect it.

subject: ai
question: Is the AI right that this classifier will give the number of cars in each photo?

artifact.explanation:
Task: count the number of cars in each parking-lot photo.
Plan: fine-tune an image classifier with classes '0-10 cars', '11-50 cars', '51+ cars' and report the class.

ai_claim: Yes. The classifier learns to recognise how full the lot looks, so its output tells you how many cars there are.

ai_solution.text: The classifier is trained on labelled photos.
It learns what lots with different numbers of cars look like.
Its predicted class gives the car count.
So it counts cars.

failure.misconception: Using a coarse classifier for a counting task
failure.explanation: The classifier outputs a bin, not a count: '11-50 cars' cannot distinguish 12 from 49. Counting needs object detection (count the boxes), density-map regression, or a model trained to output a number.
failure.why_convincing: The classifier is related to 'how many', so it seems to answer the question.

canonical_solution: No: it outputs coarse bins. Use object detection (count boxes) or count regression.

valid_evidence.summary: A photo with 12 cars and one with 49 get the same output.
Choose the model type to match the output required: counts need detection or regression.

counterexamples: The output cannot say whether there are 12 or 49 cars.

hints.text: Ask what the model outputs.
Step 3 treats a bin as a count.
Match the model's output type to the task.
Consider photos with 12 and 49 cars.
Step 3 is wrong: bins are not counts. Use detection or regression.

repair: Use an object detector and count detections, or train a density/count regression model.
debrief: Task framing decides model type: classification, detection, segmentation and regression answer different questions.

subject: ai
question: Is the AI right that segmentation, not bounding-box detection, is the appropriate approach here?

artifact.explanation:
Task: measure the area of skin lesions in dermatology photos to track growth.
Plan: use a segmentation model that labels each pixel as lesion or skin, then compute area from the pixel count and the image scale.

ai_claim: Yes. A bounding box includes skin around irregular lesions, inflating the area. Segmentation outlines the lesion pixel by pixel, so pixel counts times the known scale give its actual area.

ai_solution.text: Lesions are irregularly shaped.
A bounding box covers the lesion plus surrounding skin.
Segmentation classifies each pixel, tracing the lesion's outline.
Pixel count x area per pixel gives the lesion's area.

canonical_solution: Correct. Area measurement needs per-pixel masks; boxes overestimate irregular shapes. (A scale reference in each photo is required to convert pixels to mm^2.)

valid_evidence.summary: For a circular lesion, the bounding box area is 4/pi = 1.27 times the true area.

hints.text: Compare a box with the shape it contains.
Step 2 explains why boxes overestimate.
Segmentation outputs masks; detection outputs boxes.
Compute box area versus circle area.
This solution is correct. Segmentation measures area; boxes inflate it. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Choose the output granularity the task needs: labels, boxes or masks.
